claims.text: Differences in deformation and failure behavior among the quinary alloy and its quaternary and ternary subsets arise primarily from local chemical ordering.
Local chemical ordering alters the stacking-fault-energy landscape.
Changes in the stacking-fault-energy landscape alter the operative dislocation mechanisms.
Specific elemental-pair interactions in the quinary alloy produce a broader local stacking-fault-energy distribution than in the simpler subsets.
The quinary alloy has greater lattice distortion than the quaternary and ternary subsets.
A broader local stacking-fault-energy distribution and enhanced lattice distortion lead to higher strain hardening.
A broader local stacking-fault-energy distribution and enhanced lattice distortion delay necking.
Identical thermomechanical processing can provide comparable grain sizes and defect densities across the compared alloys.
Preferential elemental interactions in the quinary alloy promote a heterogeneous stacking-fault-energy distribution.
The heterogeneous stacking-fault-energy distribution affects dislocation nucleation.
The heterogeneous stacking-fault-energy distribution affects dislocation cross-slip.
The heterogeneous stacking-fault-energy distribution affects deformation twinning activity.
Quaternary and ternary subsets have diminished preferential elemental interactions relative to the quinary alloy.
Relative to the quinary alloy, the quaternary and ternary alloys will exhibit lower strain-hardening rates.
Relative to the quinary alloy, the quaternary and ternary alloys will exhibit earlier necking or failure.
The quaternary and ternary alloys will have narrower stacking-fault-energy distributions than the quinary alloy.
The quinary alloy has the most robust local chemical ordering among the compared alloys.
The proposed relationship is limited to equiatomic, single-phase FCC alloys produced under identical thermomechanical conditions and tested at room temperature and modest strain rates.
